<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
{ The potential energy of the Hamiltonian \eqref{FPU} is unbounded
  from below, but displays a local minimum at the origin. As a
  consequence, if $E$ is small enough, the constant energy surface
  $\{H=E\}$ contains an invariant compact connected component
  $\Sigma_E$ surrounding the origin. Thus in particular each solution of the Hamilton equations starting on it is global. One can easily show that the condition on $E$ ensuring the existence of $\Sigma_E$ is $0<E<2/3$.}
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{main.1}
For any $0<\delta\ll1$ there exists a positive constant $C$ with the
following property. For any $s\in\mathbb N$, with $2s<N$ and for any $\theta_*\in\left(0,\frac\pi
2 -\delta\right)$, and any $\epsilon\in(0,1)$, if the initial
datum fulfills
\begin{align}
  \label{ini}
&\hat p_k(0)=\hat q_k(0)=0\quad
\text{if}\quad \theta_*<\theta_k<\pi-\theta_* \ ;
\\
  \label{ini.2}
&{\mathcal{E}}:=H_2(p(0),q(0))<\frac{1}{C}\min\left\{\sin^{4s/\epsilon}\theta_*;s^{-\frac{2}{1-\epsilon}}\right\}\ ,
\end{align}
then,
\begin{align}
  \label{ss}
\forall \theta\in\left(\theta_*,\frac{\pi}{2}-\delta\right)
\end{align}
one has
\begin{align}
  \label{great}
\frac{{\mathcal{E}}_\theta(t)}{{\mathcal{E}}}\leq
C\left(\frac{\sin\theta_*}{\sin\theta}\right)^{2s} \ ,\quad |t|\leq
\frac{1}{C{\mathcal{E}}^{1-\epsilon/2} }\ .
\end{align}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
{ One easily shows that the relation between ${\mathcal{E}}$ - the initial value of the quadratic energy - and the total energy $E$ is ${\mathcal{E}}=E+O(E^{3/2})$.}
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
\label{decay}
The above theorem shows in particular that the energy in any packet of
modes with wave number $\theta>\theta_*$ decays as a large
power of the ratio $sin\theta_*/\sin\theta$, showing that the energy
resides in the modes with wave number smaller
than $\theta_*$, up to an error of the order ${\mathcal{E}}^{\epsilon/2}$.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
\label{uniformi}
We stress that all the constants appearing in Theorem \ref{main.1} are uniform with respect to 
$N$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
\label{tempi}
The times of validity of the estimate \eqref{great} are the typical
ones covered by averaging theorems, but we actually do not know if the
result can be obtained by the methods of perturbation theory or if the
actual time of persistence of the FPUT packet is longer than what we
ensure.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
\label{thermo}
Our proof does not survive the thermodynamic limit. {Apart from the fact that the Hamiltonian \eqref{FPU} is unbounded from below when $E$ is large, even adding a quartic stabilizing term to $H$, in order to get 
results in this limit we guess that the introduction of some
probabilistic tools might be necessary}. We do not have clear ideas on how to implement
such a procedure at present.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{main}
For any $s\in\mathbb N$ with $2s<N$,  there exists a linear combination ${\mathcal{I}}^{(s)}$ of the form 
\eqref{linear.comb} with the property that its Taylor expansion at
$p=q=0$ restricted to the hypersurface $P=0=Q$ has the form
\begin{equation}
  \label{espando}
{\mathcal{I}}^{(s)}(p,q)={\mathcal{I}}^{(s)}_0+{\mathcal{I}}^{(s)}_2(p,q)+{\mathcal{R}}^{(s)}(p,q)\ ,
\end{equation}
where ${\mathcal{I}}^{(s)}_0$ is independent of $(p,q)$, the quadratic part
${\mathcal{I}}^{(s)}_2$ is given by
\begin{equation}
  \label{parte.lin}
{\mathcal{I}}^{(s)}_2(p,q)={\sum_{k=1}^{N-1} \sin^{2s}\theta_k\, E_k}
  \end{equation}
and there exist a positive $C$ and a positive $R_*$ independent of
$s$ and $N$ s.t. for $R< R_*$ one has 
\begin{align}
  \label{sti.resto}
\sup_{\|(p,q)\| \leq R}\left|{\mathcal{R}}^{(s)}(p,q)\right|&< s\, C\,  R^{3}\ .
\\
\label{sti.resto.dr}
\sup_{\|(p,q)\| \leq R}\left|d{\mathcal{R}}^{(s)}(p,q)[Y]\right|&< s\, C\,
R^2\left\| Y\right\|\ .
\end{align}
The coefficients $c_{s,l}$ are explicitly given by
\begin{equation}
  \label{coeff}
c_{s,l}=\frac{(-1)^l\, (2s+1)!\, l!}{4^s s!(s-l)!(2l+1)!}\ .
  \end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{no1}
The fact that the part of $J^{(2m)}$ linear in $p,q$ vanishes on the
surface $P=0=Q$ was proved in \cite{GMMP20}.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
\label{noi_no}
In the case of the original integrals $J^{(2m)}$ (cf. \eqref{J2m}) our
method would produce an estimate of the remainder of the form
\eqref{sti.resto} and \eqref{sti.resto.dr} whose r.h.s. would contain
$2^{2m} C$ in place of $sC$. This is due to the fact that the spectrum
of $L(0,0)$ asymptotically fills $[-2,2]$.  This estimate would be
useless to our purposes.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{GMP}[Lemma 3.7 of \cite{GMMP20}]
Let us consider the Toda integral $J^{(2m)}$ and its Taylor expansion
at $p =q = 0$: it takes the form
\begin{equation}
\label{Jm.exp}
J^{(2m)}(p, q) = J^{(2m)}_0 + J^{(2m)}_1(p,q)+J^{(2m)}_2(p,q)+  J^{(2m)}_{\geq 3}(p,q),
\end{equation}
where 
$ J^{(2m)}_0=
c \in \mathbb R $, $J^{(2m)}_1(p,q)$ is linear in $(p,q)$ and vanishes on the
surface $P=Q=0$.
$J^{(2m)}_2(p,q)$ is quadratic in $(p,q)$ and has the form 
\begin{equation}
\label{Jm2.struct}
J^{(2m)}_2(p,q) = 
  \sum_{i,j}p_i  A^{(2m)}_{i,j} p_j + \sum_{i,j} r_i  A^{(2m)}_{i.j} r_j 
\end{equation}
with $A^{(2m)}$ a  symmetric  $N \times N$  matrix.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{L0}
 The $N$ (complex, orthonormal) eigenvectors ${\bf e}_k$ and eigenvalues $\lambda_k$ of $L_0$ 
  ($k=0,\dots,N-1$) are given by
  \begin{align}
&({\bf e}_k)_j:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}e^{-i j2\theta_k}\ ;\ \ (j=0,\dots,N-1) \label{eigenvec}\\
&\lambda_k=2\cos(2\theta_k) \label{eigenval}\ .
    \end{align}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{parte.quad}
Let $P$ be a polynomial and let ${\mathcal{I}}:=\operatorname{Tr}(P(L))$, then the part of
${\mathcal{I}}$ quadratic in $p$ is given by
\begin{equation}
  \label{parte.2.p}
{\frac{1}{2}}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{k_1=0}^{N-1}
\frac{P'(\lambda_{k_1+k})-P'(\lambda_{k_1})}{\lambda_{k_1+k}-\lambda_{k_1}}\right)
{ \left|\hat p_k\right|^2}\ ,
\end{equation}
with the convention that when $\lambda_{k_1}=\lambda_{k_1+k}$ the fraction
is $P''(\lambda_{k_1})$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{cotri.Bj}Assume $2s<N$, then
  the quadratic part of $\operatorname{Tr}(B_j(L))$ is
  \begin{equation}
    \label{qua.bj}
{\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}W_j(\theta_k)E_k}\ ,
  \end{equation}
  where
  \begin{equation}
    \label{wj}
    W_j(\theta)=\frac{\sin(2j+1)\theta}{\sin\theta}
    =1+2\sum_{n=1}^j\cos(2n\theta)\ .
  \end{equation}
Therefore, the quadratic part of $\operatorname{Tr}(P(L))$ with $P=\sum_{j=0}^s
  \gamma_jB_j $ is given by
  \begin{equation}
    \label{qua.bj.1}
{\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\left[\sum_{j=0}^s\gamma_jW_j(\theta_k)\right] E_k}.
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{gamma.1}
  The coefficients such that \eqref{gamma} holds true are explicitly given by
  \begin{equation}
    \label{gamma.2}
\gamma_{s,j}:=\frac{(-1)^j}{4^s}\begin{pmatrix}
  2s+1\\ s-j\end{pmatrix} \ .
    \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{prossima}
Let  $P_s$ be the polynomial s.t.
\begin{equation}
  \label{cor.W}
P_s'(x)=\sum_{j=1}^s \frac{(-1)^j}{4^s}\begin{pmatrix}
  2s+1\\ s-j\end{pmatrix} 2T_{2j+1}\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)\ ,
\end{equation}
then the quadratic part of $\operatorname{Tr}(P_s(L))$ is given by
\eqref{parte.lin}.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{HS}
One has
\begin{align}
 \label{HS.1}
 \left\| X_n\right\|_{HS}&\leq C_n\left\|(p,q)\right\|^n\ ,\quad n=1,2
 \\
 \label{HS.2}
 \left\| X_3\right\|_{S^1}&\leq C_3\left\|(p,q)\right\|^n.
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{gauss.3}
  Define the polynomial $Q_s(z)$ by $P'_s(x)=xQ_s(x^2)$, then one has
  \begin{equation}
    \label{gauss.4}
Q_s(z)=A_{s}\null\,\null_2\kern-1pt F_{1}\null\left(-s,1;\frac{3}{2};\frac{z}{4}\right)\ ,
  \end{equation}
  with
  $$
A_s:=\frac{2s+1}{4^s}\binom{2s}s\ .
$$
Furthermore, one has
\begin{equation}
  \label{gauss.6}
\null\,\null_2\kern-1pt F_{1}\null\left(-s,1;\frac{3}{2};z\right)=\frac{1}{2}\int_0^1\frac{(1-tz)^s}
      {\sqrt{1-t}}dt\ . 
  \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:main-estimates}
Let $0<\delta<\sqrt{2}-1$. There exists a constant
$C_\delta>0$, independent of $s$ and $y$, such that for every $s\ge 3$ and every
$y\in(-\delta,1+\delta)$,
\begin{equation}
 |F(y)|\le \frac{C_\delta}{\sqrt{s}}\ ;
\label{eq:F-estimate}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
 |F'(y)|\le C_\delta\ ;
\label{eq:Fprime-estimate}
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}
 |F''(y)|\le C_\delta \sqrt{s}\ ;
\label{eq:Fsecond-estimate}
\end{equation}
Moreover, defining
\begin{equation}
 G(y):=\int_0^y F(u)\,du \ ,
\label{eq:G-explicit}
\end{equation}
one has
\begin{equation}
 |G(y)|\le C_\delta \frac{\log(2+s)}{s}\ .
\label{eq:G-estimate}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{main.lemma}
There exist positive constants $R_*$ and $C$, s.t. if the initial
datum ${(p(0),q(0))}$ fulfills
\begin{equation}
  \label{R0}
R:=\left\|{(p(0),q(0))}\right\|< R_*\ ,
\end{equation}
then
\begin{equation}
  \label{scelta.s}
\forall\epsilon\in(0,1)\ \ ,\ \ \forall s\in\mathbb N
\ s.t.\ s\leq\min\left\{\frac{ N}{2};\frac{1}{C R^{1-\epsilon}}\right\}\ , 
\end{equation}
one has
\begin{equation}
  \label{main.lemma.1}
{\mathcal{I}}^{(s)}_2(t)\leq {\mathcal{I}}^{(s)}_2(0)+CR^{2+\epsilon}\ ,\quad \forall
\left|t\right|\leq \frac{1}{CR^{2-\epsilon}}\ .
  \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{divided.1}
Let $P$ be a polynomial and let $X$ be self-adjoint with matrix
elements $X_{q,q'}$ on the basis of the eigenvectors of $A$. Define
\begin{equation}
 F(t):=\operatorname{Tr} P(A+tX)\ ,
\end{equation}
then one has
\begin{equation}
  \label{divided.2}
 F''(0)=\sum_{q,q'}
 \frac{P'(\lambda_q)-P'(\lambda_{q'})}{\lambda_q-\lambda_{q'}}X_{qq'}X_{q'q},
\end{equation}
with the convention that if $\lambda_q=\lambda_{q'}$, then
  $$
 \frac{P'(\lambda_q)-P'(\lambda_{q'})}{\lambda_q-\lambda_{q'}}:=P''(\lambda_q)\ .   $$
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{C.1}
Let ${\mathcal{H}}$ be a real Banach space, let $U\subset {\mathcal{H}}$ be open, and let
\[
f:U\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}
\]
be of class $C^k(U)$. Fix $x_0\in U$ and $X\in{\mathcal{H}}$ s.t. $x_0+tX\in
U$, $\forall t\in[0,1]$. For $k\geq 2,$ we define the remainder of order $k$ of the Taylor expansion by
\begin{equation}
\mathcal R_k(x_0,X)
:=
f(x_0+X)
-
\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}\frac{1}{j!}\,
 d^jf(x_0)\bigl[\underbrace{X,\ldots,X}_{j\text{ times}}\bigr].
\label{eq:remainder-definition}
\end{equation}
Then, for $Y\in{\mathcal{H}}$, one has
\begin{equation}
{
 d_X\mathcal R_k(x_0,X)[Y]
=
\frac{1}{(k-2)!}
\int_0^1
(1-t)^{k-2}
 d^kf(x_0+tX)\bigl[\underbrace{X,\ldots,X}_{k-1\text{ times}},Y\bigr] \,dt
}.
\label{eq:main-formula}
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{th.PSS}[Theorem 1.1 of \cite{PSS13}]
Let $n\in\mathbb{N}$. Let $A$ be a self-adjoint bounded operator and let $X$ be a self-adjoint operator in $S^{n}$. Denote
$$A_t:=A+tX\ , \quad 0\leq t\leq 1\ .$$  Let
$f\in\bigcap_{k=0}^{n}W_k$. Denote
\begin{align}
  \label{}
  F(A+X):=\operatorname{Tr}(f(A+X))
  \\
  \label{C.4}
  {\mathcal{R}}_n (A,X):=F(A+X)-\left.\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{k!}
\frac{d^k}{dt^k}\bigl[F(A_t)\bigr]\right|_{t=0}.
\end{align}
Then there is a unique function
$\eta_n=\eta_{n,A,X}\in L^1(\mathbb R)$ depending only on $n,A,X$ such that
\begin{equation*}
  {\mathcal{R}}_n (A,X)
=\int_{\mathbb{R}} f^{(n)}(t)\eta_n(t)\,dt
\end{equation*}
and
\begin{equation}
  \label{stima.eta}
\left\|\eta_n \right\|_{L^1}\leq c_n\left\| X\right\|_{S^n}^n,
\end{equation}
with $c_n$ which, for any $n$ is  absolute constant.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{C.33} Let $f$ be as above.
  For all $Y\in HS$ one has
  \begin{equation}
    \label{siffresto}
\left|d{\mathcal{R}}_n(A,X)Y\right|\leq C\left\|f^{(n)}\right\|_{L^\infty}\left\|
X\right\|_{HS} ^{n-1}\left\| Y\right\|_{HS}\ .
    \end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor.PSS}
Let $A$ and $X$ and $Y$ be selfadjoint matrices s.t. the spectrum of $A_t$ is
contained in a segment $[a,b]$. Let $\delta>0$ be a positive
parameter. 
Let $P\in C^\infty(\mathbb R)$ and denote
\begin{equation}
  \label{polu}
{\mathcal{R}}_{P,n}(a,X):=\operatorname{Tr} \left( P(A+X)-\left.\sum_{k=0}^{n-1}\frac{1}{k!}
\frac{d^k}{dt^k}\bigl[P(A_t)\bigr]\right|_{t=0}\right)
  \end{equation}
then one has
\begin{align}
  \label{sti.tra.1}
\left|{\mathcal{R}}_{P,n}(a,X)\right| 
\leq
C_\delta
\left(\sup_{l=0,...,,n}\sup_{x\in[a-\delta,b+\delta]}\left|P^{(l)}(x)\right| \right)
\left\|X\right\|_{S^n}^n\ 
\\
\left|d{\mathcal{R}}_{P,n}(a,X)Y\right|  
\leq
C_\delta
\left(\sup_{l=0,...,,n}\sup_{x\in[a-\delta,b+\delta]}\left|P^{(l)}(x)\right| \right)
\left\|X\right\|_{HS}^{n-1}\left\| Y\right\|_{HS}\ .
\end{align}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{Ssl}
  Define
\begin{equation}
S_{s,l}:=\sum_{j=l}^{s}
\frac{(2s+1)!(2j+1)(j+l)!}
{(s-j)!(s+j+1)!(j-l)!}.
\end{equation}
Then one has 
\begin{equation}
{S_{s,l}=\frac{l!(2s+1)!}{s!(s-l)!}}.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
